utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies today, and Mr. Djordjevic has some more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Mr. Djordjevic [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, today I will continue with my questions starting with the point we left off yesterday. Do you know anything, although you said that you were not in Izbica on the 24th of March, do you know that all young men left Izbica and took to the mountains on the 25th of March, around 3 a.m.? Do you have any knowledge regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, when you provided information about your family on several occasions, you said you had nine children, sons and daughters. Were your sons with you in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have six sons and three daughters. Three of my sons were with me as well as two of my daughters. The others were abroad. They lived and worked abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The three sons that resided with you in Kosovo, on that day did they accompany you to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we went together to Izbice. Two stayed with us once the elder took to the mountains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is any of your sons' name Ramadani?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, the two sons who did not go to the mountains, were they in Izbica on the day of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you whether there were any other men, save for those who were taken away, you told me that there were no other men.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you whether in addition to the 150 men for whom you said had been separated from the women, you said that there were 15.000 women and to that you said yes; but now you say that two of your sons were with you in Izbica on the day of the massacre. You said they were there, therefore, I'm asking you this: You told me that there were no other men there except for those who were taken away in the two groups. Now it turns out that your two sons were there. I'm asking you now, therefore, why didn't you mention that there were any other men there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say it before, all a seven members of my family were there. They were children at the time. I did not describe them as men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were they at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was 13. The other, 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thaqi, the man you described as commander, you described as being somewhat younger, between 27 and 30 years of age. You also said that he wore a green camouflage uniform. You said he had two radio devices on him. In one statement you said that he had a large nose, whereas yesterday you said that his nose had been broken. What I wanted to ask you about this person is the following: Did you see whether he had any insignia on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been saying the same thing all along. I did not know how old he was, but from what I was able to estimate, he was in the range of 27 to 30, not sure about it, and I know that he had a large nose and a bit crooked. His eyes were greenish in colour, and I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any insignia on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, he did, but I can't recall at this stage. I did not dare look at it properly; we were not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, one of your fellow survivors, Mr. Mustafa Dragaj, described that person as being older, wearing a blue uniform and a blue helmet in his testimony to this Tribunal. Did he have in mind the same person or another person whom you may have also seen?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking on behalf of me and my group when we were seated there. The person who gave the command was the one who I've described, and I don't know who Mustafa has been describing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, on that day, did you notice anyone, out of the 80 soldiers and policemen, wearing a helmet?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A helmet? Is it a helmet you are talking about? I don't know this word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the interpreters to explain to you what the word helmet means. I know the words for it in English, but not in Albanian unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember seeing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people you saw, what did they have on their heads?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had their hats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hats worn by the police in the army. I don't know how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The way you saw them. Mr. Thaqi, you said that your oldest son took to the mountains. How old was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did he leave for the mountains, your oldest son? Why did he not stay with you in the meadow?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was scared that he would be killed. I told him to stay, but he said he would be better off leaving, and I think he made a good choice because he would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other young men, did they also leave for the mountains?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly did. There were quite a few of them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they leave for the mountains?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left before dawn on the Saturday, not in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on the 25th of March at dawn?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was on the 27th of March or before the dawn of the 28th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who decided that the young men should take to the mountains?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did it themselves because they had heard things, they were scared, and that's why they left. I, myself, was unable to restrain them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, would I be right in saying that Izbica was considered free territory since up until that time no Serb forces had reached it?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Serbian forces until I went there, and even when we went to Izbice, there weren't any. They came, however, two days later on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that in the environs of Izbica there was serious fighting between Serb forces and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about it because we lived in a valley. There weren't any gun-shots on the day until they arrived. We weren't able it to hear anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the village of Ovcarevo lies?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is it? Close to what village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the sequence Doricevc-lower Kopiliq-Asareve- Trica-Pluzhina-Likovci-Ujmiri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that in Ovcarevo there was a KLA presence, have you any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but I never saw them with my own eyes. That's what they said, but I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Saban Dragaj spend his time there since we agreed that you heard of him as being a commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never followed them and neither do I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thaqi, tell me this, please: Do you recall the statement you gave to an investigator of this Tribunal on the 20th of October, 2001, as well as the 17th of October, 2001? The investigator's name was Annette Murtagh.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember their names. There were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall having given a statement on the 17th of October, 2001, and the 20th of October, 2001, on two occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know that there was someone called Angeli [phoen] in my own house; that's who I gave my statement to and everything that I knew. Maybe I did give another one, but I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up an exhibit which later was assigned Exhibit P820. It's an aerial image. I would kindly ask for the original, the pristine copy to be displayed, not the one marked by the witness. It is the photograph MT HM 1. Otherwise it's a 65 ter 244. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, did you see this photograph yesterday for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it for the first time yesterday. There were three before, but I can't remember what year it was. We went together to Izbice, and I told them that this had happened here and there and then they made their own drawings or something like that. I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To ask you yet again, did you ever see this photograph before as well as the markings on it? The A, B, C, D, and E? Have a close look, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it yesterday for the first time. As I mentioned it earlier, there were three of them who took me to the graveyard and to the place where the execution occurred, and then they made their drawings, but I don't know any more about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, in the statement that you signed, as I've already told you, on the 20th of October, 2001, it says that you saw this photograph at the time and that you signed it at the back and apparently you even entered a date. And then you explained what the points A, B, C, D, and E meant. You talked about a group --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said it, those three people came, they took me to this place, and then I made these notes, the A, B, C, and Ds, i.e., showing how many groups there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you put these markings on, A, B, C, D, and E?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make them myself, but I did indicate that this where was the first group, the second, the third, and the fourth, and they did the writing, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did see this photograph after all, Mr. Thaqi. My next question is this: I'm not going to suggest that you look at the statement that you signed -- go ahead, please say what you were going to say. You wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see this photograph, but I described the place in Izbice where the events occurred to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it's not clear to me. You spoke earlier about A, B, C, D, and E, about the groups of people - I don't know how many groups there were, four or five, I forgot what you said - and somehow that is not consistent with what we heard earlier. So could you please clarify it for us?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the first group was the A, the B, the C, and the D. We were four groups there. This is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the statement on the screen. 65 ter 2246, please. After all, I will have to do this. Could we see the English version and the Albanian version. The English version page 14, the Albanian version page 12 on the statement, please. Now, could you please zoom in in the Albanian version onto the signature of Mr. Thaqi, just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this your signature, Mr. Thaqi? And do you see it in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the first page of the statement. This is the 1999 statement. This is not the right document. And we need the 2001 statement. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this your signature? It is, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we see the first page of that statement, both in the English and in the other version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my signature, I signed it. But I see it here 2002, you are saying 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, not this one, please. We need page 14 in the English version and page 12 in the Albanian. 14 in the English. And the next page in the English, the very beginning of the statement. This is just the sheet listing personal details. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to read the text in Albanian on the screen, Mr. Thaqi, or do you need it to be zoomed in?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, yes, it's better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you please read out the first paragraph. You say there the following: "I have signed my name and dated the back of this photograph." Is this your statement? That's what you say here.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this statement for which you claim that you have signed it, and you just confirmed your signature, we see something different from what you told us earlier today. It says here that you put your signature on the reverse of this photograph that we saw earlier. So you signed your name on the back, and you dated it. Once again I'm asking you whether this is your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my statement as I can see my signature there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you will agree with me that you did see the photograph after all, that you did sign it on the reverse, and even put the date on it; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the photograph then. I don't know that. I only know that I described the location where the events occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read out loudly the first paragraph, please. Can I ask you to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. "I have already made a statement to investigator Nigel Stewart from the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague on the 9th and 10th of November, 2000. I now wish to make this statement..." I think it's enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the way to the end, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do you want me to read it to the end? I did give this statement, and there's no need for me to read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We need you to read the bit that's important to me. So would you please read out the entire first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not read this part. I'm an old and ill person, don't make me read it to the end. The whole world knows what happened there and what massacres and rapes were committed there. So please don't make me read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, as a human being, I feel regret for everything that took place, and I want you to believe when I say this; but in doing my duty here, I wish us to discover the truth, and the truth at this moment is something that doesn't suit you. So this is why you are refusing to read out this paragraph until the end. So let me read it out for you. "I wish to give an additional statement" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, comments like that is not appropriate, it is my submission at this time. That type of comment to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Carry on, please, Mr. Djordjevic. You were going to read now to the balance of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I now wish to make this additional statement today to investigator Annette Murtagh in relation to the aerial photograph she has shown me with the identification number 'MT AM 1' on it. I have signed this photograph and put the date on the back." This is what you stated in your statement, Mr. Thaqi. A lot could be said in the cross-examination, but I will conclude it here in respect of your age and everything else. Mr. Thaqi, in this statement you said, and you also mentioned in your testimony here, these points, A, B, C, D, and E. Why did you mention them? You were mentioning some groups, and we heard from you here that there was a group that was split into two, so now I don't understand these groups A, B, C, D, and E. This is completely inconsistent with what we've heard from you yesterday. So could you please briefly explain it.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, there were two groups here, the right and the left side. On the left side there were three groups. The first group was my group, the second, the third, and the fourth were on the right side. So please don't make me go over this again now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, I have already told you that I feel just as uncomfortable as you do. We did not hear such comments from you while my learned friend was examining you. You came here to give evidence and this is why I'm putting these questions to you. Why did you not mention four groups yesterday, rather you mentioned two. Could you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained everything. They divided us into two groups, the left side had three groups. I don't know how many were in the other groups. But in my group there were 33 persons. So on the right side there was one group and on the left side there were three groups, one after another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We did not hear that from you yesterday, but I will not be questioning you in that direction anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we please admit into evidence, not the entire statement of this witness, just the first three paragraphs, both on the English page on and the Albanian page, both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you'll have to choose, either the whole of the statement or just nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'll choose the whole statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received. We are dealing with the statement dated the 17th and 20th of October, 2001; is that correct? It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: On that will be assigned D00123, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not be needing this photograph anymore. We know that the Trial Chamber will bear in mind what the Defence said on that issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, the next portion of my questions and the topics that we will be covering will not take very long, but I think it's important to clarify them. Yesterday you said that there were 147 victims of this massacre and that you took part in their funeral. I would like to know the following: My learned friend, Mr. Stamp, asked you about Dr. Liri Loshi. What I want to ask you about Dr. Loshi is this: In relation to the day when the funeral took place, when did you see him? Was it on that day, day prior to that day, day after to that? So please orient yourself in relation to the day of the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day of the funeral was a Wednesday. I wouldn't know the date, but it was March, it was a Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you see Dr. Loshi was it on Tuesday, Monday; or was it on Thursday and Friday? And also, Mr. Thaqi, who took the footage that we saw with you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said Wednesday, I believe -- I think it was the 31st of March. It was a Wednesday, three days after the execution. Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, it was on the fourth day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Thaqi. Then we'll agree that you saw Dr. Loshi on the day of the burial, the funeral; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, you told us yesterday that 147 victims were buried, or rather, you said that that's how many there were. Dr. Loshi compiled a list which has been admitted into evidence here - I think this is P292. Dr. Loshi said that there were 127 corpses. Could you explain the difference in numbers, Dr. Loshi said 127, and you claim 147. And later on we will come to the bit where it will become clear why that is important.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, some villagers from other villages came and collected the bodies of their family members and buried them in their own cemeteries. What I'm saying, you have it all on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question for you, Mr. Thaqi. All these people who were buried that day, on Wednesday, were buried, as you have told us, in a process organised by the KLA. What did you mean when you said that it was organised by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that the KLA organised the burial. What I said was that the KLA and family members of the victims helped us bury the victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, would you agree with me that among the corpses that were buried, there were also some bodies that had been brought in from other locations and were not just the corpses that were involved in the event of the 28th of March in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is not correct. They didn't bring bodies from other locations to be buried there. Only Serbs could move the bodies, not us. We would never do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't say that you transported the bodies. I just asked you whether, among those buried there, were there also people who died, who were killed, or perished in any other way in other locations? That's what I asked you. We did hear some other testimonies that I'm not going to put to you now.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a graveyard at all. A person from Izbice who owned a meadow gave the meadow for these victims to be buried there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will have to ask you something in relation to the statement that you gave in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Chamber for a bit of indulgence, I need to find the reference. I need the number in Albanian. 65 ter 2246. Let me give you the page number. So this is the Albanian statement, and we will need the portion -- last page, both in the English and in the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will naturally first have to ask you whether you gave this statement. This is the interpreter's certification, so we need the last page of the statement. Then a bit more back. This is not the right statement. The text here is in the Serbian. This is probably the 2001 statement which has been admitted into evidence because it mentions point D and point E on the text that's on the screens. That's not the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the exhibit, the 65 ter number that was used, contains both statements. The earlier one is towards the front, and the later one is -- succeeds that one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now please give the statement in Albanian to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you please turn to the last page. Third paragraph: "Four days after the massacre in Izbica it was a Wednesday, the 1st of April. I learned that the Serbs were no longer in Izbica and that the burial of the victims was taken place." That is to say that you didn't organise it, you learned of it; am I right? I'm now putting this statement to you where you say I learned that the burial was in progress. Am I right in stating that you came after having heard that the victims are being buried, and then you go on to say how you went to help. So am I right in stating this?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Klladernice village. Young men from Izbice came and said that the victims were going to be buried that day in Izbice. I went there, I had a piece of bread and cheese with me. When I arrived there, the burial had already started. 20 had already been buried, and there were many people there, family members, KLA members, and others. We buried the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you again if this is your statement.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The same paragraph towards the end you say there: "The burial of the victims was organised by the KLA. Altogether there was a total of 147 victims of the Serb massacre. Some of the bodies were taken by their families and buried elsewhere. 130 were buried in the field in Izbica. During that day, I met up with Jetish," et cetera, et cetera. Today I asked you what it meant that the burial was organised by the KLA. In your answer you said, No, they were only present there. You said so today. You said "we buried them." Here I can see that you were informed of it and then you arrived there. So I'm asking you which is correct: That the burial was organised by the KLA, as you say in 1999; or is it true what you said a decade later, that is to say that you organised the burial of the victims of the massacre, as you call it.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who organised it. There were many people present including KLA members and civilians, and I don't know what else to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given that you said at the time that the burial was organised at the time by the KLA, that is why I'm asking you this question now. Why did you say so at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying the same all the time. I don't know who organised it, but I'm saying that the KLA did take part in the burial, and I don't have anything else to add. The whole world is aware of what you were able to carry out, of the worst of the worst which cannot be seen anywhere else in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, were there any Serb families in your village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When do you mean? What time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just prior to the war, Mr. Thaqi, before NATO bombardment in 1999, 1998, 1997?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been no Serbs in my village for 38 years. Before 1998, however, with the exception of the police and the army that roamed about, there was nobody inhabiting there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the villages neighbouring yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Grapc outside Broje, there is no one in Vojnik there are -- there were Serbs in Belince, in Polan, and surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which families those were, how many were there, what were their last names?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I saw them from time to time, but I wasn't familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any Serb families nowadays in that village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some have returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, as of 1998 and 1999 and later, did you get by any information on the kidnapping of Serb civilians and the murders of police and soldiers prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard about it. Maybe they were kidnapped, but I never heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not hear about it. Very well. Mr. Thaqi, before you is your 1999 statement. I have a Serbian text in front of me, and we have the same text in English and Albanian. Since the paging -- the pagination does not correspond fully, I tried to number the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The portion I'm looking for should be on page 2, but starting with the first paragraph where it says "witness statement" that would be the 13th paragraph. In the Serbian version it is the sixth paragraph on that page. I don't know what paragraph it is in the Albanian. In any case, if you start from the beginning it is paragraph 13 in all three languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go back to your statement -- to your description yesterday concerning the arrival of three members of the police as you said so. They went to the "kruska" village, set a haystack on fire, and then demanded money. You mentioned that yesterday at page 16 of the transcript at lines 9 to 12 referring to the three policemen. And you said that two of them wore green camouflage uniforms, blueish in terms of hue, and the third one wore a plain blue uniform. Two of them, therefore, you say wore green-blueish camouflage uniforms, and one had a plain blue uniform. However, in your statement in the paragraph number 13 of the statement of 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are being too fast and too long, and I'm having some difficulty understanding you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no other way for me to explain the context. The context is as follows: Yesterday you said that two of them had greenish/blueish camouflage uniform, whereas the third one wore a plain blue uniform. That's what you said yesterday. However in your 1999 statement you say -- THE INTERPRETERS: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have the reference for --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already given the reference, my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If the reference is page 16, line 10, or thereabouts yesterday, that is not -- what is quoted is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 17, line 2 and line 3. When we talked about colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, it is the 13th paragraph from the beginning, you conclude that paragraph by saying they wore green-olive camouflage uniforms with similar coloured caps, they had belts of ammunition around their chest on over their shoulders. They spoke Serbian. The camouflage colour of the uniform is similar to the one depicted in the top right of the chart shown to me by Investigator Stewart. You were shown that colour as well as -- by my learned friend, Mr. Stamp. It was on the chart. How did we arrive at that colour, whereas a decade ago you said three men in green camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think for this witness, the question is much too conjoined with other suggestions, and there are just too many statements in the one question. I object to it because it is overly complicated and needs to be simplified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, you have in front of you a statement you made in November 1999. Do you see that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It says 2002 here. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you look at the second page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you see a paragraph that says that, "at about 9.30 in the morning, most of the people were eating beside their tractors."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not yet, but that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could look to see if you can find that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is number 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is number 14 if you have a numbered version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. Now, if you look well over halfway through that paragraph, you will see that you speak of men wearing green-olive camouflage uniforms. In paragraph 14. Can you find that reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, but I'm not sure I understand you very well. It says: "After a few minutes, a number of policemen came on foot and they took" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A little before that, in the previous paragraph, do you see where it is written, "the men with Kalashnikovs were wearing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- green camouflage."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did find it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is speaking, it appears, of the three policemen whom you first saw setting fire to a haystack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were three policemen. I don't know who of them set the fire, but there were three of them. And then they went downhill from the meadow onto the road, and that was the time when I went because they kept asking for money and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the point you are being asked about is that you describe those three policemen as wearing green-olive camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand this. That was the colours of the police uniforms. I don't know how to say it differently, but what I said is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were the three policemen all wearing the same uniform? Same type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One had a different uniform, the other two had the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what was different on the uniform of the one policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying it was different. I don't know how to describe how it was different, but it was camouflage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What's written in the statement seems to indicate that they were all wearing the same type of uniform. Can you help us to understand why you didn't mention that one of them was wearing a different uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember exactly, but what I said then was meant to describe what I saw at the time. I now tend to forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've got to try and decide whether the three of them were wearing green-olive camouflage uniforms or whether one of the three was wearing a different sort of camouflage uniform. Are you able to be sure in your mind today about the uniforms that these three men were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that one of them had a different pattern, but I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was there any difference in the colour of the uniform for this one man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was similar, but I think that the camouflage was of a more dense pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, that may have helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to a great extent. The only thing I wanted to ask the witness is if he recalls what we said in terms of uniform colour of the three men in the Milosevic case and what he stated in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have all of that, of course, and we will assess that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, before I move on to another topic, I wanted to ask you this. Are you quite certain that you can tell different colours?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't ask me about this again. That's what it was, and I've spoken about it. The whole world knows about it. Please don't mistreat me any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I just make it clear, Mr. Djordjevic, I was mistaken. We have not received as an exhibit the transcript in the Milosevic trial or in the Milutinovic trial, so we don't have any direct reference to any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was warned to that effect by my assistant. I would kindly ask that both transcripts be admitted into evidence, both from the Milutinovic and the Milosevic case precisely because of the testimony we heard today and yesterday. And I ask for the transcripts to be admitted in total concerning the reference of this witness's testimony. It is 65 ter 2247 in the Milosevic case and 65 ter 25 -- 5038 [as interpreted] in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will each be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 2247, Your Honours, will be assigned D00124. And 65 ter -- could Mr. Djordjevic please repeat the other 65 ter number for the Milutinovic transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 5039 -- no, 8, sorry. 5038 in the Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00125, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, since I do not wish to press matters any further in terms of cross-examination since the witness said that I was mistreating him, I'd rather him -- have him have a rest. I would like to tender the 1999 statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, will be assigned D00126.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this may be a good time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic. THE INTERPRETERS: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, will you please tell me this, can you tell colours?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said it earlier, I am done with the colours. Please don't ask me further. I have nothing else to say. I think I'm done with the subject. I keep forgetting, you know, what happened on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's quite clear to me, however, Mr. Thaqi, given that you did not wish to answer my question, you are now forcing me to put the following question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the transcript from the Milutinovic case, which is D125. Could we have is on the screens please, page 2294. Line 10 and 11. Page 2294, which is page 10. That's right. Page 10 and 11. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Thaqi, when you testified in the Milutinovic case, when asked by one of my colleagues, or rather, he asked you about the nationality or ethnic background of these three persons whose uniforms we discussed, and then in reply you said this: "I don't know the nationality, but I know that they were dressed in black." That's what you said. And this is why I asked you whether you could tell colours, and you did not wish to reply to that. Now, would you please tell me what did you mean when you said that they were dressed in black? You didn't even claim that they were dressed in camouflage uniforms or anything of the sort, you just said black. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that they were dark skinned, but not that they wore dark or black clothing. Only that their faces were darkened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, at the time you said: "... I know that they were dressed in black, they were dark-skinned." That's what you said. But you also said that they were dressed in black. How come?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a mistake. It's been recorded wrong. I don't think I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Thaqi, would you please explain to us how did you find out that these three men were policemen? Based on what did you learn this? Did somebody tell you this perhaps? You claim they were policemen. Why do you claim so? Why don't you claim that they were soldiers or paramilitaries? No, you said specifically policemen.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The uniform meant they were policemen. What nationality and who they were, I don't know, but their clothing suggested they were policemen. Nobody told me; I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the uniform like that Serb policemen wear? Is it a green uniform or a black one, or a blue one? What did these soldiers wear then?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe it, but the policeman that I saw yesterday here on the screen, that's what they wore. I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That policeman wore a blue camouflage uniform, and today you told us that it was a kind of a green uniform but that one of them was a denser type. You did mention yesterday a blue uniform, I have to admit that, so can I, based on all that, conclude that you assumed they were policemen without actually knowing that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed they were. I did not dare ask them what they were or talk to them at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly what I asked you. Now, let us leave these three policemen aside and go back to the main person, as you told us, because he kept talking on two radios all the time. You say that he wore a green camouflage uniform. To your mind, what was he? Was he a policeman or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to me, he was a soldier. I don't know, I didn't ask about his background or anything of that, but based on the uniform, that's what I concluded. Nobody told me anything about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, allow me, please, to remind you what you stated in the Milutinovic case. Page 2295.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see it on our screens, please. It reflects your evidence. Line 2, 3, 4, and then 11, 12, 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You describe this man here, or rather you are replying to questions put to you by one of counsel, and then today you told me "I didn't dare look, I didn't take a good look." But back then in lines 11, 12, and 13, you said that he wore the same insignia as the Yugoslav Army he was about 160 centimetres tall, he was quite fat, he had green eyes, and he had a broken nose. He was between 27 and 30 years of age. So does this refresh your memory because in this evidence here you claim that you saw the insignia of the Yugoslav Army on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to see, but I did not focus in the details you describe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely why I'm putting this to you. You said that you could see the insignia of the Yugoslav Army. What did you mean when you said that? What were the typical Yugoslav Army insignia that you mentioned? Which insignia of the Yugoslav Army did you have in mind? Could you help us with that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the -- he was a captain or something of the sort, or something called "Porucnik."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thaqi, let us go back to an unpleasant moment, both for you and all of us. That was the moment when the men started firing at you. You have already described this man, so I'm not going to ask you to go over that a again, but I will ask you whether, according to you, he was dressed as a soldier, or as a policeman, as a member of the paramilitary forces, or something different?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to me, he was a policeman in camouflage uniform. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he wore a green uniform, so why do you think that he was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the uniform. I didn't ask him. But that's what we knew about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a green camouflage uniform, if I'm not mistaken. That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is correct. Don't harass me any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, it is not my intention to mistreat you, rather, I wish to establish who the direct perpetrator was. I believe this to be an important point both for justice and for the victims. I do not wish to ask you to apologise to me, because I can understand your sentiments, but I need to ask you to explain to me how you know that this man was a policeman. You seem to be quite sure of that. So could you please explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the police clothing. I didn't ask him what he was or who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Thaqi, this is my next question: You have mentioned paramilitaries, were there any paramilitaries among those 80 men?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how did you distinguish that army from the regular army and police, as you call them? How could you tell who was who?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the clothing and on the hat which had a five-pointed star on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five-pointed star, are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, "Petokraka." I don't know how to describe it. They had a hat with a visor, and had something which I don't know how to describe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did you have any direct contact with that army? Did you personally have any contact with them?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mixed up together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that these were members of the paramilitary forces, or were they perhaps members of some special units? What colour was their uniform, Mr. Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same colour as the army's. I don't know how to describe it. I'd be able to tell you if I could see it on the screen though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the predominant colour of those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Thaqi, now that we are dealing with these 80 men who arrived via fields and reached your group, tell me, please, whether among those men, Serbs, you were able to recognise somebody among the troops that had arrived to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we conclude that among the members of those Serb forces there were no local Serbs who had been called up into the army from local towns and villages?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they came from villages or towns, I don't know. All I know is that they came there, and they were mixed up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was referring to nearby villages in Kosovo, I wasn't referring to Serbian towns and villages in Serbia proper. I was trying to say that there were no residents of villages and towns in Kosovo, the nearby ones.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to tell whether they were locals or not. I didn't know anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thaqi, if you can please explain to us, we saw on the screen here a list of persons who were together with you when the man whom you claim was a member of the Serb forces shot at you. And there were two names there. I think these names are Azem and Muharrem. And next to them there was the last name Thaqi written in and then that last name was crossed out and then another last name was written, Osmani. Was there a mistake there, and can you explain it? Yesterday you were reading out their names.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I made the mistake because we were referring to them by their father's name Muharrem and Azem Thaqi. In fact their surname is Muharrem, Osmani and Azemi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, I'm going to ask you to clarify some other illogical parts of your statement. Perhaps they're not illogical if you can explain. Yesterday as you were describing the events in Izbica, you told us that you to -- shelling which one could hear, you were unable to sleep throughout the night and so on, and that in the morning you heard voices of Serbs in the forest. Today you told us that the young men had left on the same morning. Was the reason for young men leaving, the noise that you heard? Or was the reason for their leaving the fact that the town or village was being surrounded because they left on the 28th at dawn? So could you please tell us what was the reason for the young men leaving?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think counsel had better get the proper reference and relate the evidence as it was said by the witness, because I don't think that what is said about the evidence is entirely correct, and that could confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend, I tried to save us some time, but I will need to spend that time in order to give you a reference to yesterday's evidence of this witness. He said that he heard the voices of Serbs in the forest. Just a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like to ask the witness, in order to save time, when did you hear the voices of Serbs, of Serbian army in the forest? Can you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear any voices. I said we heard gun-shots at 2.00 in the morning. We were trying to get some sleep, me and Uka the one who was killed. I got up at the time, and Uka said, What are you up to? And I said, They have surrounded us, they have arrived and surrounded us. And he said, No, get down and get some sleep. And that's exactly what I said. I don't have to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you this because the Prosecutor intervened, otherwise I would not have. In any case, we can agree you said that since you confirmed it. Can you tell me what was the date, that was the morning of what day in March?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it before, this was on the Saturday in the night, which means the 28th. It was a quarter to 2.00 in the morning. It was before dawn on the Sunday, the 28th. That's what I said, and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is what I originally asserted. You said that in the morning the young men went to the mountains at dawn on the 28th; am I correct? Did you indeed say so today?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left beginning from the 26th when we went there. Whoever could, left. I can't speak here of everyone who left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is this: The fact that you realised that you were surrounded, was that the reason why the young men took to the mountains? Or perhaps not?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some left earlier, some later, because they were afraid of being killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you mentioned the village of Belica, it is a Serb populated village as you said at page 11, line 15 of yesterday's transcript, I believe. You said that all of the Serbs from that village joined the paramilitary forces. How come you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody said so because personally I didn't know either of them. From Leqina, Polan, or other villages. They simply attacked us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who attacked you?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is known who. Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are discussing the village of Belica, we will not go any broader than that. I'm asking you whether the inhabitants of Belica attacked you. You seemed to be silent on that. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all Serbs. They were in unison. They were orchestrated by Belgrade because otherwise they wouldn't be in a position to be in uniform. I couldn't recognise whether they were from Belica or Belgrade, but that's how everybody said, and I believe that was true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Albanians were also organised in Kosovo and that they were directed by someone as this was the rumour among the public? Do you know anything about that, and if so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who directed the Albanians, but they were also organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this sincere answer. My next question has to do with that precisely. Among the soldiers who arrived that day, the 80 people, did you notice any Chetniks as you yourself used the term?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to describe the paramilitaries as Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then all is clear. It seems that it was your name for them. Mr. Thaqi, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm through with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Stamp, do you re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a couple -- THE INTERPRETERS: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could bring back on screen the aerial photograph, 65 ter number is 0244, but the Exhibit number ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There were some questions being put to you, Mr. Thaqi, about when was it you first saw the photograph. I just want to clear up any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we firstly move to page 2. Do we have page 2 of that photograph there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a minute. I just want to show you something to refresh your memory, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think we need to turn this around so you could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your signature is there, is that it, Mr. Thaqi, at the back of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And with the date, did you write that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So just take your time and relax. Can you, on the basis of what you are seeing now, recall if the photograph might have been shown to you at that interview in November 2001 or October 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I'm not sure. I think, yes. I think it was in my own home when they showed it to me. And then from my home we went together to Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we now return to the face of the photograph, or the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could look at it this way just for a minute, I know you prefer to have it inverted, but I just want to ask you this: Do you recall when I was asking you questions yesterday, you proceeded or attempted to tell about other places where persons were killed, and I stopped you and told you to stick to what you personally saw and observed? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first group, yes, I saw it with my own eyes. I was one of them. 30 people were killed. The second group was 20 metres away below. It was like an elevated place. They didn't see us. There is a pear tree to this day. The third group was, again, 20 metres higher. We remained in between the two groups in that area and Hajzir Kotorri survived from that group and then he was shot when he went was trying to flee towards the mountain. And the other group was on the other hand, 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, your statement of October 2001 is in evidence where you described the groups that the arrows and the letters on this photograph designate, those areas where the killings occurred. But what I want to ask you is this -- is apart from point A, or the vicinity of point A where your group was shot, did you personally see the shooting in respect to the other groups that you have referred to in your statement, and that the photograph, the numbers in the photograph relate to?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see the actual shooting because I was laying prostrate for 40 minutes, but I only heard the shots, and I'm repeating it that I heard the shots fired at the second, third, and fourth group. I only heard the shots. When everything was quiet, I dared to look up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the groups referred to in your statement of October 2001 that were killed, and in your statement you have them at point B, point C, point D, and point E, when did you discover the exact location where they were shot? When did you discover that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discovered that, first I heard, I told you, the shots, but I found out when we buried them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in the course of the cross-examination, you answered quite a lot of questions about colours and uniforms, and you did accept that it is very he difficult for you to describe them verbally by calling out the colour, the name of the colours, but you can identify them from the picture or from pictures. And you did say that the three --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you did say that the three men that you saw first, or at least some of them, wore the uniform in the picture I showed you yesterday, and that is P316.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at it quickly again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to describe or to tell me what colour it is, I just want you to say of all of the 80 plus men in the field, the armed Serbian forces in the field on the 28th of March, how many wore the uniform that you see this man here in the photograph attired in?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them. I can't give you an exact figure, but I would say about 25, maybe more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many of them did you see with this "milicija" insignia on the sleeve?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say the exact number. I believe all of them had. It was a very difficult moment for anyone to dare look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that. And were these dressed like this person, this figure here, did they receive and follow orders issued by the person that you describe as the "commander"?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know, but I only know that he ordered us in relation to -- ordered them in relation to us to send -- to take us to this place and to kill us. Otherwise, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else there issuing orders to the armed men who were in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is all, Mr. Thaqi. Thank you very much. And thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, may I say a few words before I leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that when the Defence lawyer asked me, I think that if he were in my place, he wouldn't be able to say anything given the fact that we were killed, our children were killed, we were forced to leave Kosova, and many other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thaqi. Well, as you've gathered, you -- the questions for you have ended --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honours. I think all the world knows what happened to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We thank you for being able to come here again and assisting us. We know you've been times before. We thank you for the help you've been able to give us, and you may now of course return to your family and your ordinary affairs. The court officer will help you out, Mr. Thaqi. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The court officer now will help you out, Mr. Thaqi, and we thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we proceed with the last witness, I wonder if I might raise an ancillary matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P6 -- sorry. The document identified as 65 ter number 615 is a Kosovo atlas, and it was a document I think that the parties could have agreed upon earlier, but we have been moving so quickly we haven't had a chance to meet and discuss things as much as we should. We have and we have agreed that with the review of the evidence, the ongoing review of evidence by the Court, especially of the 92 bis and 92 ter evidence, we have various witness reference to place names in Kosovo. It would be useful at this stage, in fact earlier perhaps in the course of the proceedings, if the entire atlas with their index and so forth was received in evidence for the benefit of the Court, to assist the Court. There were some pages at the beginning of the atlas which learned counsel for the Defence, I think quite rightly, indicated that they perhaps should not be included, and we have removed those six pages and wish to tender together the atlas, minus those six pages, and ask that it be received in evidence, and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We thank you for that, counsel for both sides, and we receive the atlas minus six pages. The court officer is concerned that he doesn't know which six pages it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that is -- I should have informed him. We already removed it from the document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we receive the whole document in e-court, which is the atlas minus six page that have been removed by consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned P00823.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are we now ready for the next witness, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And that will be Ms. D'Ascoli who will have conduct of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please read aloud the affirmation on the card given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. D'Ascoli has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, this witness's evidence relates to paragraph 72 (J) and 73 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you please state your full name and your date and place of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: My name is Bajram Bucaliu, I was born on the 16th of June, 1957, in Slakovc e Eperme, Gnjilan municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to move a bit closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can the microphones be adjusted so they are closer to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, where are you currently living?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Currently, I live in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: In Ferizaj town?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And where were you living in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: In March 1999, I used to live in Staro Selo in the vicinity of Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, could you tell us which is your current occupation, please?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Now I work at the train station of Gurez.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Is this in the Ferizaj municipality, well, is this close to Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: It is 9 kilometres from the train station in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And did you also provide a second statement in August 2001?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I also gave another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review both statements?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that was made possible for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the information contained in these two statements is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge and recollection everything in the statement is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender into evidence both witness statements please, and the 1999 statement is the 65 ter number 02298 while the statement from 2001 is the 65 ter number 02299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 02298 from the 1999 statement, Your Honours, will be assigned P00824. And 65 ter number 02299 for the 2001 statement will be assigned P00825.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying in the Milosevic case in 2002?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And did you also testify before this Tribunal in the Milutinovic et al. case in September 2006?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review your previous testimonies in both cases?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I have had the possibility to look into the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if today you were asked the same questions that you were asked in the Milosevic case and in the Milutinovic cases, would you provide substantially the same answers and testify in the same way?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, the answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender into evidence also the testimonies of this witness. The Milosevic transcript is the 65 ter number 02287, while the transcript of the witness in the Milutinovic case is the 65 ter number 05191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The evidence in the Milosevic trial will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P00826, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the evidence in the Milutinovic trial will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P00827, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now read a summary of this witness evidence. The witness comes from the village of Staro Selo in the Ferizaj municipality of Kosovo. On 2 April 1999 his village was occupied by the VJ with soldiers and military tanks. The army stayed until 5 April 1999 when paramilitaries entered the village. Some of them entered the witness's yard, threatened him, and ordered him not to leave the village. They also established a curfew in the village, according to which people were not allowed to leave their houses between 7 p.m. and 7 a.m. In the evening of 13 April, 1999, paramilitary soldiers went to an Albanian house, killed three people, and deported four others. The witness and other villagers heard of this fact. As a result, the following day, almost the whole village gathered in the centre of Staro Selo and started leaving on foot for Ferizaj. On 15 April, 1999, the witness boarded a train with his family. He estimates that there were thousands of people on the train. The train headed towards Djeneral Jankovic, but was at some point sent back to Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down while reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. The following day on 16 April, 1999, the witness and other thousands of people boarded again a train at the Ferizaj railway station. Serb policemen also boarded the train. After Djeneral Jankovic and close to the Macedonian border, people were ordered off the train, and policemen told them to walk on the railway tracks to the Macedonian border. As they walked along the tracks, the soldiers and policemen were shouting insults at them. The witness and his family crossed the border into Macedonia that day, and they were taken by bus to a refugee camp. From 1987 until the 25th of March 1999, the witness worked at the Ferizaj railway station, therefore, he also illustrates the log-book or diary used to keep track of train circulation at the Ferizaj railway station from the 1st of January, 1999, until 19th of June, 1999. He explained what is recorded in the log-book, and the circulation of trains in normal times and in those days of March/April 1999. That is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, I will now ask some questions to clarify certain aspects of your evidence. Mr. Bucaliu, at page 2, paragraph 3 - this is both in the English and the B/C/S version of your first statement of 1999 - you say that your village of Staro Selo was first occupied on the 2nd of April by VJ soldiers. And you specify in the same paragraph that the soldiers who entered the village occupied six houses belonging to Albanians. During your testimony in the Milutinovic case --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And for the record, this is transcript pages 3014, 3015.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: -- you specified that you saw that from your house. Is that correct? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a hand-drawn map.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
