utterances.text: The 65 ter number is 00043. If I can have it on the screen, please. Could you please enlarge the upper part of the map. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise this drawing because I made it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So is it the map of your village, of Staro Selo; correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking this is what my village, Staro Selo or Fshati i Vjeter looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to locate your house on this map, approximately where it was located?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could the usher please provide him with ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I use --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: You could put a dot or a sign close to it?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This is my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The circle, for the record, indicates the witness house.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, are you also able to indicate on the map where the Albanian houses, where the soldiers were staying, are located? The houses that the soldiers occupied on the 2nd of April upon their arrival. If you could put an X close to the area.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: For the record, and X and two lines are indicating the position of the Albanian houses on the two sides of the road. Thank you. Your Honour, can I please have this -- can I please tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00828, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, let's now move to the 5th of April. At page 3 first paragraph of the English version of your 1999 statement, you say that on the 5th of April, the army left the village; and you further say in the following paragraphs that on the same day later in the afternoon, paramilitary forces entered your village, some of them came to your yard, threatened you, checked your tractor and ordered you not to leave the village. Going to paragraph 3 of the same page in referring to the paragraph military forces, you say, and I quote: "We were terrified by these knives and their behaviour in general." Can you please clarify what you mean by this and what type of behaviour they had that terrified you.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Your Honours, everything mentioned by the lady is true. When I say that we were scared, we were scared by the ominous appearance they had. They were people who would make you sad even today were you come across them, let alone during that time. They were people who were unshaved, who had big, big beards and hair, and who had irregular clothing, who had knives which were not regular army knives, but the knives that you use to butcher animals. We saw knifes that were still -- had blood on them. What they had -- what they had on their heads was something that is call Kokarda, used by the -- hats used by the Chetniks. And from our knowledge of what the Chetniks had been able to do in the past, we were anticipating that the same horrible things would be coming our way too.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I ask you who are you describing now in this detailed description that you just gave us?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This is a description of what was called the paramilitary forces. They used to call themselves Chetnik forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And could you give us some example of the behaviour that they had and that was terrifying to you?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Excuse me. For instance, my first contact with these paramilitaries was on the 5th of April in the afternoon. I was sitting on the stairs to my house, given that I had heard at the time that paramilitary Chetnik forces had entered the village, and so we were fearful of what might occur. So I was sitting on the stairs to my house when from the courtyard of my next door house which was my brother's house - there's three of us living in the same compound - I was able to see three of them enter. So from the -- I was able to see, for instance, one of the children of my brother's move the curtain away to be able to see what was happening, and one of them trained the automatic rifle in that direction. I don't know whether out of fear or something else, but I reacted, I stood up and said please don't, it's a child. And at that stage, that person said -- asked me who I was and I said, I am a member of this family, I am the brother. He asked me to go there. Asked about my ID, which I showed to him. And the first question that he asked was, Where is your tractor? To which I said it is behind the house, behind the barn where we kept the animals, the cow-shed. And he said, Let's go and see where it is. And with the automatic rifle trained on my back, he led me there, i.e., behind the cow-shed, and my wife, my late wife now, fainted at that stage because she thought that I was going to be assassinated, and then he asked, he said, you know, Why -- what have you got in the tractor? Why have you prepared the tractor? And so on and so forth. This is a long conversation which I don't think I need to give any details on.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's move on to the 14th of April when you and your other villagers left Staro Selo and went to Urosevac town. How far is Ferizaj Urosevac from your village, from Staro Selo?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The village is at a distance from 3 to 4 kilometres so it is a distance of 4 kilometres from my house to the centre of Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, sir, at page 4, paragraph 1, of the 2001 statement, you described what you saw in Ferizaj town when you arrived there with your family on the 14th of April. You mention having seen tanks in the centre of the town and check-points throughout the town. Can you please clarify who manned those check-points?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The place is called the bridge which is at the crossroads between the main road from Prishtina to Skopje and Ferizaj to Gnjilan. There was always a check-point there which was manned all the time by police and army forces. It was a permanent check-point where people were checked, things were taken from them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Were there other check-points around the town or in Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. In numerous places inside the town. But this was a more regular check-point, for instance, on the day when we returned from Hani i Elizit we were able to see many check-points across the town. But this -- another regular check-point was in the village of Gerlice a check-point that had been in place for a very long time, a period of two to three years and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The other check-points that you mentioned and that you saw on the 14th of April in Ferizaj town, by which forces were they manned?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: As I said, there were many across the town, almost at every crossroads or main road there were these forces. They were manned by police and army troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, at page 5 of your 1999 statement, you say that you first boarded a train at the Ferizaj railway station on the 15th of April, and then a second time another train the following day on the 16th of April, which is when you finally reached the border to Macedonia. Sir, can you explain briefly why you boarded the train two times, first on the 15th and then on the 16th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: During the first time on the 15th of April, we boarded the train and forgive me for repeating here, there was a large crowd of people who managed to get on and the larger one who had to stay behind at the Ferizaj train station. We went to the train station at Hani i Elizit, which is on the border of Macedonia where we were kept for approximately four hours on board the train. I had the privilege to be able to contact the chief of the station given than I worked for the railways, and I knew my colleague Vule, and I asked him continually why are we being kept waiting, and he said that we are establishing contacts with Macedonian authorities, who for the time being, are not allowing us to cross and that is why we have to wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you please slow down in answering because I think that the interpreters might have problems in translating. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Thank you, I shall try.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So you said that basically the Macedonian authorities didn't allow you the train to proceed farther, and that's why the train was sent back. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's what the chief of the station and my colleague Vule told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And then you went back to the station and boarded a train for the second time on the 16th of April. Why did you want to leave, or why did you board those trains, sir?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: We wanted to board the train to escape with our life because what happened in my village, let alone in the entire territory of Kosova, we were able to withstand the insults, provocations and all, the opening of trenches by young men in the village, the looting; but when the killings started, it was a question of survival. So we wanted to escape in order to be safe. We wanted to save our children, the other members of the family, that's why we turned our back on our houses. That's why we left our houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement and also today in answering one of my questions, you mentioned many people in your statement you specify thousands of people being there at the train station both times you boarded the train. Can I ask you what was the ethnicity of all those people?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: There were all Albanians who wanted to flee with their lives intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can you describe the conditions on the train you boarded both on the 15th and the 16th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Luckily, when I boarded the train, we were able to take passenger trains, even though there were people who had to make the same journey on board freight trains. The conditions were awful, there were far too many of us. We were packed like sardines in a manner of speaking, by which I mean to say there were so many people and the conditions were not great during that journey. However, we were satisfied if only to be able to cross the border and be safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, did you see any forces on the train that you boarded?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: There were policemen on the train, Serb policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Were those forces armed?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, they had light weaponry. Some of them had automatic rifles, others had pistols.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And on the 16th of April when you boarded the second train, then you were ordered after Djeneral Jankovic to get off the train. Can you please tell the Court where you were at that point and who gave this order to get off the train?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: What I said was that the 16th of April we reached the train station at Hani i Elizit where again I established contact with my colleague Vule who I asked would we be lucky enough today to be able to cross; and his answer was, Yes, Bajram, today you will be able to because the Macedonian authorities are accepting you, so you shall be able to get across. You will not be staying here for far too long, and we'll send you by train. The distance being 1 to 1.5 kilometres from there to the border. So I greeted my colleague and that's exactly what occurred. In about 15 or 20 minutes we left the train, proceeded up to the border where it came to a halt, and where Serb police -- police and army forces gave us orders. The soldiers were outside the road, but the policemen were with us on the train. They descended as well. They had a little chat. And then they ordered us by beckoning as well as ordering us to get off the trains, which is what we did. We stayed there for about half an hour around the train. And after approximately half an hour, we were ordered again - and I was one of the first because I was in the first carriage near the engine - and I was the first to cross. And I said you and your mother, can you get across. They said sir, go in front of the engine, you have to walk between the tracks and continue just walking between the tracks. If you go outside the tracks, the whole area has been mined, and you have to proceed that way, all the way into Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu. This place where you stopped, where the train stopped, was it a normal stop for trains? Was it a place or a station where trains would normally stop?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No, the station is at Hani i Elizit, one and a half kilometres away from the border with Macedonia. Trains don't stop at that stage. The train stopped at that stage only to allow us to descend and to proceed on foot towards Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a few questions left for the witness, but this is maybe a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, we will have the second break now and resume at 1.00. Could I remind you of something that was said a few days ago. We want to encourage all counsel to confine themselves to matters that are essential rather than just simply filling out what is in the statement unnecessarily. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm almost done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, what was your job before the war started in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Until March 1999, I used to work at the train station in Ferizaj as a cashier.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I please -- I'm going to show you a document, a book.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If I can have on the screen a 65 ter number 01331, please. Can we go through the first pages of this document, please. Of the original one.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, can you see what is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Even farther, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very small. I mean the letters are very small, if you could zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If you can continue going on through the pages, please. More. Okay. That's fine. Thank you. Could you enlarge it a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Is it better now, sir?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: If it's possible to zoom it in a little bit more, I will try.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. It is the log-book of trains that is kept at every train station.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And where was this one kept?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: There is a person who is responsible. It's called train manager. He keeps such a diary. He writes down the incoming and outgoing trains.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this one as the diary of which station?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This is the diary kept at Ferizaj train station.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you personally make entries in this particular log-book?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Not in this one because at that time I wasn't working as a train manager.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you remember at what time this -- what time this log-book refers to?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This page, for example, as you can see from the date, you can infer when. I don't know, because this is simply one page. This shows a date.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we have the front page of the original document, please, on the screen. I meant just the first page of the entire document, the front page of the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, are you familiar with how this book was used?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. I said that this was used to keep track of all the trains that passed through the Ferizaj station.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Does that mean that all trains that went through Ferizaj were recorded in this log-book?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Normally every train that passed, came, or left the station should have been recorded in the log-book. When one is finished, you get another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think we are still on page 3. Can we have the first page of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you see from this heading, from the beginning of the document which period it refers to?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. You can clearly see here it is written in Serbian language, it's a log-book, a communication log-book started on the 1st of January, 1999, and the end date is not recorded when this book was finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think that if we go to the last page of the document, we can see the last day for which entries were inserted. The previous page, please. Page 150, please. Thank you. Can you enlarge it, especially the left-hand side column. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, can you see which was the last date -- last day recorded for which entries were made in the log-book?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If you can scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is the last page, it shows that it's 19 of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the log-book is discussed and explained by the witness in great details in his previous testimonies so I won't go into further details to explain it, and I will just seek to tender it into evidence, please. This is the 65 ter number 01331.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have a large document in Serbian and eight pages in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, because the English translation only refers to the entries -- to handwritten entries in Serbian which were translated. The numbers of the trains and the times of arrival and departure are not translated, of course. At the beginning of the English translation, there is a table which translates all the columns of the documents in order to have an understanding of where and how dates are entered into the evidence. That's why we have only eight pages of English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00829, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, thank you very much for having answered my questions. I don't have further question for this witness at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Staying with the log, I wanted to ask the following: Has the entire log-book been admitted pertaining to that year or only parts of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The whole log-book has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon sir, my name is Dragoljub Djordjevic, I appear on behalf of the accused in this case. I won't have many questions of you, only a few by which I will try to clarify certain portions of your statements and your testimony today during my learned friend's examination-in-chief. My first question has to do with the paragraph 2 of your statement of the 24th and the 25th of April, 1999. It has to do with the 13 Serb families you refer to. Can you tell me the last names of those families, who they were, what they did at the time, and where are they now. There are three questions it seems. Let's start with who they were and what their last names were.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I will do my best even though a lot of time has passed and I don't remember all of them. But some I do remember. They were my neighbours, they lived in my village, we lived together for quite a long time in that village, actually until 1999. From 1964 when we settled there until 1999, we lived side by side. So I don't want to repeat things. We got on well together, we were good neighbours. Perovic was one of my neighbours on the other side was Tepascevic there were other families as well. I don't recall their last name. If I am given more time, maybe the last names may come back to my memory, but these two that I mentioned were my neighbours when I lived in the old house before I moved into the new house in another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The place you marked in answering one of my learned friend's question, does that place depict the location of your old house or the new house? And I now refer to a document which was admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The place I marked shows my new house where I lived from 1996 to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you still reside there?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No. That house was burned down, and I couldn't rebuild it, so for the moment I live in the vicinity of the train station. I have rented a house which belonged -- was a property of the railway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, as Exhibit P828.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, it is P828.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you say you remember your former neighbours and that you were in good relations. Where are they today, the Perovic and the Tepascevic families, are they back in the village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No, unfortunately they no longer live in the village. After the war was over, they moved away from the village. And to my knowledge they live outside Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As you said, before the war you enjoyed good relations with your Serb neighbours. Did your children attend school together with theirs, or did they attend different shifts and classes in the school?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: As I already said, we enjoyed very good relations with the Serb families. Unfortunately, the children didn't attend the same school because there were few Serb children, therefore they couldn't provide education only for such a small number of children, therefore, they went to Ferizaj school. During the time I was a student in Ferizaj, we used to go to the same school, but attend different classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose you probably wanted to say that you attended different shifts in terms of mornings and afternoons. I would presume you did not attend the same -- you were not in the same class given your different age?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I said we went to the same schools, but we attended separate classes because of the language. I'm talking about the time I was in school. We were together with Serb children both when we worked out in the morning and in the evening shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The curriculum, the lectures, were in Serbian or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: For Albanians the curriculum was taught in Albanian. For the Serbs, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is right. Thank you. In the same paragraph of the statement of the 24th and 25th of April, 1999, the second paragraph towards the end you say: "When the NATO air-strikes started on the 23rd of March, 1999, during the night around 8.00 p.m. electricity was turned off every night. During the night my entire family gathered together in one house and slept together." What was the reason for all of you to assemble in one house only after that date? The date may be of less importance, what is more importance is the beginning of the NATO air-strikes and the power outage. Why did you decide to stay in one house, and whose house it was? How many families were there and what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: It is true what you put to me. On the night of the air-strikes of the 24th of March, the strikes started at 2000 hours to my recollection. We were staying each at our respective homes. And then around 2300 hours, the shots started in the Ferizaj-Gnjilan main road that I drawn if my sketch, with military vehicles, with Pragas in the direction of our houses. And of course, Praga being a heavy vehicle, it fires long range, so many houses were hit by the shells. And we were afraid, therefore, we withdrew to the centre of the village. My uncles live there, that's why we moved to their houses where several families assembled. My family being one of them, along with the families of some neighbours. A total of five, six, families. This was the case with other families that moved and assembled together. That was the reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of the statement you say: "The army occupied the village for the first time on the 2nd of April, 1999, at 8.30 in the morning." How come you say that the army occupied the village? Wasn't it the army of the common state at the time? What do you mean when you say that the army "occupied" the village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That was my perception. You might use another word. You might say the entry of the military forces if you don't want to use the word "occupy." For me it seemed like an occupation, but you might as well say they entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, occupation seems to be the third term you used today. At that time of giving the statement, you said that they took up the village as if an enemy force had entered it. What did you have in mind precisely, would that be taking up or occupying the village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: As I said, that was time of war. Having heard by then what was going on in other parts of Kosova, we thought that the same thing would happen to our village, and that's why we were scared. For us taking up or occupying was the same thing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is all much clearer now. In the same paragraph you say that the military tanks arrived, dark green in colour, with tracks and no long barrels, no barrels extended. Could you please explain what the different would be between a short or an unextended and an extended long barrel? As a matter of course, did you serve your army service at all?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honours, I have a problem. I hear two voices at the same time of the Defence counsel and the interpreter. I hope I understood the question put to me. When I mentioned the long barrels, I was referring to smaller calibre weapons, not like cannons, but I was referring to tanks that had long barrels and that were of smaller calibres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same paragraph you mention your neighbour, Maksim Perovic, you said that his house was marked with 4 Ss for indication and that the other Serbian houses did not have those markings. Why was Maksim Perovic's house marked with the sign?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Most probably to be able to tell which were the Serb houses. Most probably they had some plans and wanted to spare the Serb houses. This is what we were told, that the Serbs were told to mark their houses so that the forces could tell which ones were theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is why I'm asking why only Maksim Perovic's house was marked and not the houses of other members of Serb community in the village. Who was Maksim Perovic in the village at that moment? Was he an important figure for the village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Maksim Perovic was not an important figure. I knew that he was a supporter of Seselj's radical party, and these persons who entered our village on the 5th of April declared themselves to be members of the radical forces of Seselj. However, the other Serb families refused to mark their houses with this sign because they didn't want their houses to be different from the Albanians, but Perovic accepted the proposal to mark his house, and that's why he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What happened afterwards with the remaining Serb houses that were not marked? Were they harassed?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No, during the time we were in the village, nobody harassed them. I don't know what happened after we left the village, but during the time we were still there, their houses were not -- they were not harassed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of the same statement, you go on to say that in Staro Selo there were no KLA members, Liberation Army of Kosovo. Tell me, please, were there some in the vicinity in other villages near your village and near Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: It is true that there was no KLA presence in my village, and in the surrounding villages. There was KLA presence in Bjeshket e Jezercit which is 15 kilometres of aerial distance from my village. There there was KLA presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you remember ever stating that you helped some KLA members? You stated that in another statement you gave to this Court. And how do you explain what you said back then and what you said here before this Court now?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I explained then that on one occasion following a Serb offensive in Bjeshket e Jezercit some KLA units, or, rather, some KLA members withdrew and went down to some of the villages. One of these members was a son of a colleague of mine. He had settled in Varos village. My colleague was scared that his son might get captured by the Serb forces, and most probably eliminated as a KLA member, so he asked for help in terms of taking his son to another village. This is what I meant at the time. It is true that I went by car to pick up this colleague's son, and take him to another village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, when did this offensive take place, or, rather, this fighting near Bjeshket e Jezercit?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: To my recollection, this occurred in October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, where is Varos located?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The village of Varos is south of Ferizaj about 3 kilometres away from Ferizaj, and about 3 kilometres far from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, where is Bjeshket e Jezercit located?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Bjeshket e Jezercit are north-west of Ferizaj and north-west of my village, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How far is that to the north-west of Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: About 10 or 12 kilometres from Ferizaj, and from my own village about 15 as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So we can conclude that a full six months before the KLA air-raids, there was KLA in the vicinity of Urosevac. There was fighting like the one that you just mentioned and that you were quite close in that respect with the KLA. In one of your statements you said you did not believe in KLA at all until the NATO bombing started. On now we're finding out that you started helping them 6 months prior to the bombing. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: These are two different issues. First of all, he was not an armed member of the KLA. He had abandoned the ranks of the KLA and had gone to Varos. As the son of a colleague of mine, I was obliged to help him. Not because he was a KLA member, but just because he was the son of someone I knew. I was a member of the LDK that followed a policy of peaceful resolution to problems. We believed that Kosova would become independent by peaceful means, not through employment of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Still, I have to put to you the statement that you gave on the 29th of August, 2001. That was a Wednesday. And then you continued on Friday, the 31st of August, 2001. You gave this statement to investigator Annette Murdagh. This is P825.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pull up the statement. We need page 2 both in Albanian and in English. This is paragraph 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where you say the following: "On one occasion I helped transporting a KLA soldiers from one village to another when the unit withdrew because of the strong presence of the Serb forces." You did not mention any friend of yours or anything of the sort. I accept that you were not a member of the KLA, but you did help them. And here you did not describe this person as a son of your friend or colleague rather, you just describe him as a KLA soldier, so how do you reconcile the two?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I will repeat again. He was a member of the KLA, but when I picked him up, he was not armed, and he had abandoned the KLA ranks. He might have joined the KLA later on; but at that time I assisted him, he had withdrawn from the KLA ranks. He was running away from the Serb forces, and I helped him to get it to another village from Varos. It is true that I mentioned him as a son of my colleague in my previous statements, or evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that I put to you, you say a KLA soldier. I understand that he had discarded his weapons. He may have not even had a uniform since he was hiding. But I want to know this: Do you know what KLA uniforms looked like at the time?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No, not really. Although, we had an opportunity to see them on foreign television channels wearing KLA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Hadja, the Muslim priest as he is described in your statements, Imam, told you about the killings of the Zeka family. Was that the actual reason why you left the village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, it was the reason why we left the village. We had heard about different types of terror, lootings, killings, and so forth; and when the killings actually started, every human being will try to run for his or her life. When the decision time comes whether to live or to die, people will always opt for fleeing in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will agree with you, sir. My question that will be the concluding question for today, since it's time for adjournment, will be this: Where is the Zeka family located in relation to your house that you drew in the sketch that we all saw about hour and a half ago, and also just recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pull that up on the screens again. This is P -- just a moment. P828.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark the location of the Zeka family house, please.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The Zeka family lived in two different parts. One of them, one of the Zeka families lived here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sketch, please. Could you put a letter A in the spot where part of the family lived.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the other part of the family?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Maybe about 50 to 100 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you put B there.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I don't know if we can erase the dot that I just made, and then I can mark it with a B. I can mark the A and the B again; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your house is marked with an X.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No, my house is marked with a circle. Not with an X.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Where is the A?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please scroll up in order for the witness to be able to mark. That's right. We see the Skopje-Pristina road. All right. So we see the Skopje Pristina road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, where were the houses of the Zeka family located?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How far is that from your house? If these houses have a distance of 50 metres between them, then how far are they from your house?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Most probably 500 to 600 metres from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a good time for adjournment. Could I tender into evidence this sketch with new marks. Later on we will be putting more questions related to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Markings made on P00828 in blue, Your Honours, will be assigned D00127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must adjourn now for the day, and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. The court officer will give you assistance during the break, and we will continue with your evidence tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. We now adjourn.
